questions.stem:
Nina weighed a random sample of 50 carrots from her shop and recorded the weight, in grams to the nearest gram, for each carrot. The results are summarised below.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Weight of carrot} & \text{Frequency (f)} & \text{Weight midpoint (}x\text{ grams)}\\ \hline 45\text{--}54 & 5 & 49.5\\ \hline 55\text{--}59 & 10 & 57\\ \hline 60\text{--}64 & 22 & 62\\ \hline 65\text{--}74 & 13 & 69.5\\ \hline\end{array}$

(You may use $\sum fx^2 = 192102.5$)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Use linear interpolation to estimate the median weight of these carrots.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: for a correct expression (oe) without endpoint, e.g. $(59.5)+\frac{10}{22}\times 5$. Allow "n+1" so e.g. $(59.5)+\frac{10.5}{22}\times 5$. Allow working down e.g. $(64.5)-\frac{12}{22}\times 5$. Allow $\frac{m-59.5}{64.5-59.5}=\frac{25-15}{37-15}$ oe for M1.
A1: for awrt 61.8 or, if (n+1) is used, allow awrt 61.9.
$[Q_2=] (59.5)+\frac{10}{22}\times 5 = 61.7727\ldots$ awrt $\underline{61.8}$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find an estimate for the mean weight of these carrots.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: for a correct expression for the mean $\frac{49.5\times 5+57\times 10+62\times 22+69.5\times 13}{50}$ or an attempt at $\frac{\sum fx}{50}$ with at least 3 correct products or $3000 \leqslant \sum fx \leqslant 3200$.
A1: for 61.7 from correct working.
$[\bar{x}=]\frac{\sum fx}{50}=\frac{3085}{50}=\underline{61.7}$

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Find an estimate for the standard deviation of the weights of these carrots.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: for a correct expression including square root. Ft their 61.7. Allow use of s.
A1: for awrt 5.93. Allow $s=5.989787\ldots=$ awrt 5.99.
$[\sigma_x=]\sqrt{\frac{192102.5}{50}-\bar{x}^2}=\sqrt{35.16}=5.929586\ldots$ awrt $\underline{5.93}$

parts.label: d
parts.text:
A carrot is selected at random from Nina's shop.
(d) Estimate the probability that the weight of this carrot is more than 70 grams.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) M1: for $\frac{4.5}{10}\times 13$ (use of interpolation to find the number of carrots weighing more than 70g) (may be implied by sight of 5.85, may also be implied by 50 − 44.15) (Allow 50 − 44 (=6) or 50 − 45 (=5) coming from 44.15 or 44.2 seen in working to score M1).
A1cao: for an answer of 0.117.
[Interpolation from above] $\frac{4.5}{10}\times 13 (=5.85)$. So probability is $\frac{5.85}{50}=\underline{0.117}$.
Note: Use of normal distribution scores M0A0.

questions.stem: At a school athletics day, the distances, in metres, achieved by students in the long jump are modelled by the normal distribution with mean 3.3 m and standard deviation 0.6 m

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find an estimate for the proportion of students who jump less than 2.5 m
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) 1st M1: for standardising with 2.5, 3.3 and 0.6. Allow $\pm$.
2nd M1: dep on 1st M1 for attempting $1-p$ where $0.5<p<1$.
A1: for an answer in the range 0.0912~0.0918. NB calc gives 0.09121128...
$[\text{Let } J=\text{the length of a jump}]$ $\mathrm{P}(J<2.5)=\mathrm{P}\left(Z<\frac{2.5-3.3}{0.6}\right)=\mathrm{P}(Z<-1.333\ldots)=1-0.9082=\underline{0.0912\sim0.0918}$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The long jump competition consists of 2 jumps. All the students can take part in the first jump and the 40% who jump the greatest distance in their first jump qualify for the second jump.
(b) Find an estimate for the minimum distance achieved in the first jump in order to qualify for the second jump.
Give your answer correct to 4 significant figures.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: for standardising with "d", 3.3 and 0.6 and setting equal to z ($0.2<|z|<0.3$).
1st A1: for a correct equation with compatible signs with $z=0.25$ or better, i.e. $0.253$ or $0.2533$.
2nd A1: for awrt 3.452 (calc gives 3.45200856... use of 0.2533 gives 3.45198).
$[\mathrm{P}(J>d)=0.4 \Rightarrow] \frac{d-3.3}{0.6}=0.2533$ $d=\text{awrt }\underline{3.452}$

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Find an estimate for the median distance achieved in the first jump by those who qualify for the second jump.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) 1st M1: for a correct probability statement involving 'J' and 'm' (median) only (may be implied by 2nd M1). Use the letter in the standardisation as the one representing the median.
2nd M1: for $\frac{m-3.3}{0.6}=z$ (with compatible signs) where $0.84\leqslant z \leqslant 0.85$.
A1: for awrt 3.80 (accept 3.805).
$[\mathrm{P}(J>m|J>d)\Rightarrow] \frac{\mathrm{P}(J>m)}{0.4}=0.5$ or $\mathrm{P}(J>m)=0.2$; $\frac{m-3.3}{0.6}=0.8416$. So $m=3.80496$ (calc 3.80497274...) awrt $\underline{3.80}$

parts.label: d
parts.text:
The distance of the second jump is independent of the distance of the first jump and is modelled with the same normal distribution. Students who jump a distance greater than 4.1 m in their second jump receive a certificate.
At the start of the long jump competition, a student is selected at random.
(d) Find the probability that this student will receive a certificate.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) B1ft: for an answer in range 0.0912~0.0918 or the same as part (a) for $\mathrm{P}(J>4.1)$.
M1: for $0.4\times$their $\mathrm{P}(J>4.1)$.
A1: for answer in the range 0.036~0.037 (No fractions). NB $0.4\times0.0918=0.036712$ and $0.4\times0.0912=0.03648$.
$\mathrm{P}(J>4.1)=0.0918$ (same as (a)). So $\mathrm{P}(\text{certificate})=0.4\times\text{"(a)"}=\underline{0.036\sim0.037}$

questions.stem:
The partially completed tree diagram, where $p$ and $q$ are probabilities, gives information about Andrew's journey to work each day.

$R$ represents the event that it is raining
$W$ represents the event that Andrew walks to work
$B$ represents the event that Andrew takes the bus to work
$C$ represents the event that Andrew cycles to work

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Given that $\mathrm{P}(B)=0.26$
(a) find the value of $p$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) 1st M1: for attempt at correct equation for $p$ (Must have at least 2 terms in $p$) and must be set equal to 0.26.
2nd dM1: dep on 1st M1 for solving their linear equation in $p$ by reducing to $Ap=B$ with at least 1 of $A$ or $B$ correct.
A1: for $p=0.44$ (or exact equivalent e.g. $\frac{11}{25}$).
$0.4p+0.15(1-p)=0.26$; $0.25p=0.11$; $p=\underline{0.44}$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Given also that $\mathrm{P}(R'|W)=0.175$
(b) find the value of $q$
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) 1st M1: for a probability ratio of the form $\frac{rq}{rq+(1-r)\times 0.6}$.
1st A1ft: for $r=1-$their $p$ and the $=0.175$.
2nd dM1: dep on 1st M1 for rearranging their equation into the form $Aq=B$ with at least 1 of $A$ or $B$ correct or correct ft.
2nd A1: for $q=0.1$ or an exact equivalent.
$\frac{\text{"0.56"}q}{\text{"0.56"}q+\text{"0.44"}\times 0.6}=0.175$; $0.462q=0.0462$; $q=\underline{0.1}$

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Find the probability that Andrew cycles to work.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: for $(1-\text{their }p)\times(1-0.15-\text{their }q)$.
A1: for 0.42 or an exact equivalent.
$\mathrm{P}(C)=(1-p)\times(1-0.15-q)=\text{"0.56"}\times\text{"0.75"}=\underline{0.42}$

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Given that Andrew did not cycle to work on Friday,
(d) find the probability that it was raining on Friday.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) 1st M1: for a ratio of probabilities with 0.44 or 'their (a)' on num.
2nd M1: for a ratio of probabilities with 0.58 or '1 − their (c)' on denom.
A1: for $\frac{22}{29}$ or awrt 0.759.
Correct answer only scores 3 out of 3.
Note: If correct ft on num. and denom. leads to "num" > "denom" then maximum score is M0M1A0.
$[\mathrm{P}(R|C')=] \frac{\mathrm{P}(R)}{\mathrm{P}(C')}=\frac{\text{(a)}}{1-\text{(c)}}=\frac{\text{"0.44"}}{\text{"0.58"}}=\frac{22}{29}=0.75862\ldots$ or awrt $\underline{0.759}$
